title: Traffic and Flow Diagram Automation with Claude
tagline: From ping and traceroute evidence to an approved, versioned flow diagram
audience: Network operations, NOC, load balancer, data centre and cloud network teams, and automation leads in enterprise IT in India and worldwide
prerequisites: Hands-on familiarity with ping and traceroute
Exposure to at least one load balancer or ACI fabric is helpful, not required
outcomes: Explain what ping and traceroute can and cannot prove about a traffic path, and encode those limits in the diagram
Set up Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK and an MCP server that exposes read-only probe tools for this workflow
Build deterministic Python probe runners that return typed path records Claude consumes through tool use and structured JSON outputs
Enrich hops with F5, Citrix NetScaler, Radware Alteon, other load balancers (Anaya LB) and Cisco APIC context, and render evidence-linked Mermaid diagrams
Publish diagrams to ServiceNow and GitHub behind scope limits, named approvals and an audit log, and detect path drift on a schedule

modules.title: What a flow diagram must prove, and what probes can tell you
topics: Why hand-drawn traffic diagrams go stale: the request-to-diagram cycle in real NOC and change work
What ping and traceroute actually show: ICMP and UDP probes, TTL expiry, RTT, per-hop loss, asymmetric return paths
Where evidence goes dark: firewalls that drop ICMP, load balancers that hide pool members, ECMP and MPLS hops
The teaching pattern for the course: Claude plans and explains, deterministic code probes, a person approves, everything is logged
modules.lab: Trace the path from a lab client to a lab VIP by hand, record every hop and every gap, and write the brief for the pipeline you will build.
modules.deliverable: Manual path record and pipeline brief.

modules.title: Setting up Claude Code, the Agent SDK and MCP for this workflow
topics: Claude Code project layout for the diagram pipeline: CLAUDE.md, allowed tools, repository conventions
Claude Agent SDK in Python: sessions, custom tool definitions, structured JSON outputs and permission hooks
An MCP server exposing only read-only probe tools (ping, traceroute, DNS lookup) with scope lists and logging
Secrets and credentials outside the prompt: environment variables and a vault for device API tokens
modules.lab: Stand up the MCP server, connect it to Claude Code and the Agent SDK, and prove Claude can call a probe tool but cannot run an arbitrary shell command.
modules.deliverable: Working Claude workbench with a read-only probe MCP server.

modules.title: Deterministic probe runners in Python
topics: Wrapping ping and traceroute with subprocess: timeouts, retries, max hops, packet counts and exit-code handling
Parsers for Linux and Windows output into a typed path record, with unit tests against saved captures
Handling the ugly cases: stars, duplicate hops, rate-limited routers and partially answering paths
Claude requests probes through tool use; code runs them and returns structured results
modules.lab: Implement and test the probe runners with Claude Code, inspect every diff, and run them against three lab targets with different failure modes.

modules.title: Path evidence model and structured outputs
topics: Pydantic schema for a path: source, target, hops, RTTs, loss, timestamps, probe ID and tool version
Marking unknown segments explicitly rather than filling gaps; confidence per hop
Prompting Claude to summarize a path record with mandatory citations to probe IDs
Evidence bundle layout: raw output, parsed record, Claude summary, all versioned together
modules.lab: Define the schema, feed Claude a path with missing hops, and verify the summary cites probe IDs and refuses to invent the gap.
modules.deliverable: Path evidence schema and summarization agent.

modules.title: Enriching hops with load balancer context
topics: F5: virtual servers, pools and pool members through iControl REST and tmsh list ltm virtual
Citrix NetScaler lbvserver, servicegroup and binding objects through the NITRO API
Radware Alteon virtual services via Cyber Controller and Alteon REST; a common adapter for other load balancers (Anaya LB)
Matching a hop or VIP address to a device object so the diagram can show what sits behind it
modules.lab: Build read-only adapters for the lab F5 and NetScaler, let Claude map a VIP to its pool members through tool use, and log every API call.

modules.title: Data centre fabric and cloud path context
topics: Cisco APIC REST API: tenants, bridge domains, EPGs and L3Outs that a path crosses
Reading ACI endpoint and interface data to place a hop on a leaf or border leaf
Hybrid paths: on-premises to cloud VPC or VNet, where traceroute stops and cloud route tables begin
Deciding what to enrich and what to leave as a labelled unknown
modules.lab: Query the lab APIC for the EPGs and L3Out a path traverses and attach fabric context to the evidence bundle.

modules.title: Generating the traffic and flow diagram with Mermaid
topics: Mermaid flowchart and sequence syntax for hop-by-hop traffic and request-response flow
Claude drafts the diagram from the evidence bundle; a deterministic renderer validates the syntax
Every node carries the probe ID that placed it; unknown segments are styled as unknown
Diagram conventions: VIP, pool, firewall, fabric and cloud boundary shapes and a legend
modules.lab: Generate Mermaid for the lab path, render it, break the evidence on purpose and watch the renderer reject an unsupported node.

modules.title: Guardrails, approvals and audit for probing and publishing
topics: Scope lists: which prefixes and hostnames may be probed, enforced in code not in the prompt
Rate limits and probe budgets so automated tracing never becomes a ping storm
Named approver required before a diagram is written to the CMDB or merged into a shared repository
Audit log of every tool call, device API query, model output and approval decision
modules.lab: Add scope enforcement, rate limits and an approval gate, then attempt an out-of-scope probe and an unapproved publish and show both are refused and logged.

modules.title: Publishing to ServiceNow and GitHub
topics: ServiceNow Table API to update the incident, change or CI record that requested the diagram, and the Attachment API to attach the diagram and evidence bundle to it
Flow Designer trigger: a request record starts the pipeline and receives the result
GitHub pull request with the Mermaid file, evidence bundle and Claude-written summary; a person reviews and merges
Repository layout for diagrams per application and per site
modules.lab: Run the pipeline from a ServiceNow request to a GitHub pull request and complete the approval end to end.

modules.title: Drift detection and scheduled re-mapping
topics: GitHub Actions schedule that re-runs probes within scope and compares against the published path
Deterministic diff of path records; Claude explains the change in plain language
Opening a pull request only when a path changed, with the diff and evidence attached
Operator runbook: false drift from ECMP, maintenance windows and probe failures
modules.lab: Schedule the re-mapping job, change the lab path, and review the drift pull request Claude explains.

modules.title: Capstone: request to approved flow diagram, end to end
topics: A ServiceNow request in, probes run, hops enriched across F5, NetScaler, Radware, other load balancers (Anaya LB) and ACI, Mermaid diagram out
No publication without a named approver; audit trail reviewed
Acceptance criteria, limitations statement and team demo
modules.deliverable: End-to-end traffic and flow diagram pipeline.

capstone: A repeatable pipeline that takes a flow diagram request from ServiceNow, runs ping and traceroute through deterministic code, enriches every hop from load balancer and ACI APIs, has Claude draft an evidence-linked Mermaid diagram, and publishes it to ServiceNow and GitHub only after a named approval, with drift detection on a schedule.

narration: hook

A ticket asks for the traffic flow from the branch office to the payments V I P. Someone opens a terminal, runs traceroute, runs ping, and starts drawing boxes by hand. By the time the diagram is finished, the path has already changed.
hook

What if Claude ran the probes through code you trust, read every hop as evidence, and drew the diagram for you, with a person approving before anything is published? That is traffic and flow diagram automation, done with Claude, done safely.
intro
Gennoor Tech presents Traffic and Flow Diagram Automation with Claude.
story

One request in. One proven diagram out. Over three days you build a pipeline in eleven modules where Claude plans and explains, deterministic Python runs ping and traceroute, and every hop in the picture traces back to a probe you can replay. Claude never guesses a path. If a hop did not answer, the diagram says so.
path0

You begin with what traceroute and ping can actually prove, and what they cannot. Asymmetric return paths. Load balancers that hide pool members. Firewalls that drop I C M P. Then you set up the workbench. Claude Code on your machine, the Claude Agent S D K in Python, and an M C P server that exposes only read only probe tools, with every call logged and credentials kept out of the prompt.
path0

Next you build the probe runners. Deterministic Python wrappers around ping and traceroute, with timeouts, retries and parsers that turn raw output into a typed path record. Claude requests the probes through tool use and receives structured J S O N. It cannot run a shell command on its own. And when a hop returns stars, the record marks it unknown instead of filling the gap.
path1

Day two adds context. Hops are enriched from F5 through iControl REST and t m s h, from Citrix NetScaler through the NITRO A P I, from Radware Alteon and Cyber Controller, and from other load balancers, Anaya L B included, through a common adapter. The Cisco A P I C tells you where a path enters the A C I fabric. Then Claude writes Mermaid. A deterministic renderer validates the syntax, every node carries the probe I D that placed it, and unknown segments are drawn as unknown.
path2

Then the module most teams skip. Guardrails. Probe targets are restricted to an approved scope list, enforced in code and not in the prompt. Rate limits and probe budgets keep automated tracing from becoming a ping storm on production links. Any diagram going to the C M D B or into a shared repository needs a named approver, and every tool call, device query and decision lands in an audit log you can hand to a reviewer.
path3

Day three is publishing. The result is written to the ServiceNow incident, change or request record through the Table A P I, with the diagram and its evidence bundle attached through the Attachment A P I, and Flow Designer starting the pipeline. A GitHub pull request carries the Mermaid file, the evidence and a summary Claude wrote, and a person reviews and merges it.
path3

Then drift. A GitHub Actions schedule re-runs the probes within scope, compares the new path with the published one, and opens a pull request with a diff only when something changed. Claude explains the difference in plain language. You decide what to do with it. The capstone ties it all together, from request to approved diagram, with nothing published that a person did not sign off.
labs

Every lab runs in a contained environment with lab load balancers, a lab A P I C and fictional hostnames. You will watch a traceroute go dark behind a firewall, see Claude mark it unknown instead of inventing a hop, and reject a publish that has no approver.
stats
Eleven build modules. Three days, hands on. Four device families enriched. And zero hops drawn without evidence behind them.
who
